title: Schema design, Postgres specifics and zero-downtime migrations
seriesDescription: Schema design and Postgres, scaling and multi-tenancy, MongoDB and Redis, consistency, warehouses and vector search. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Normal forms vs denormalisation, JSONB and GIN, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, replica lag, and the expand-and-contract recipe for changing a live schema.
source: PostgreSQL 16 documentation (JSONB, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE, partial indexes, partitioning); Use The Index, Luke; Designing Data-Intensive Applications; Stripe and GitHub engineering blogs on online migrations

questions.prompt: A table `order_items(order_id, product_id, product_name, qty)` has key `(order_id, product_id)`. `product_name` depends only on `product_id`. Which normal form does this violate, and what is the fix?

options.text: 2NF (partial dependency): move `product_name` into a `products` table keyed by `product_id`.
options.why: Right: a non-key column depends on only part of the composite key, which is exactly the 2NF violation.
1NF is about atomic values and no repeating groups; `product_name` is already atomic.

options.text: BCNF only: add a surrogate key and leave the data as is.
options.why: A surrogate key does not remove the duplicated `product_name`; the partial dependency is still there.

options.text: No violation: duplicated names are fine as long as an index exists.
options.why: An index does not stop update anomalies when the name changes.

questions.explanation: Partial dependency on part of a composite key = 2NF violation. Fix by moving the dependent column to the table keyed by the determinant. Interviewers then ask "when would you deliberately undo this?" (read-heavy snapshot of the name at purchase time).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Copying `customer_name` into every row of `orders` speeds up the order list page but creates update anomalies.
questions.reason: The same fact is now stored in many places, so a change has to be applied to every copy or the copies disagree.

whys.a: Correct: duplication is the cause of the anomaly, so R explains A.
whys.b: R is not just true, it is the direct mechanism of the anomaly.
whys.c: R is true, so A cannot be an A-true-R-false case.
whys.d: A is true; denormalisation does trade write complexity for read speed.

questions.explanation: Denormalisation trades write cost and consistency risk for fewer joins. Keep the normalised source of truth and treat copies as derived. Some copies are correct on purpose, for example a price captured at order time.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Normalising a schema always makes every query faster.
questions.reason: Normalisation removes redundancy, so an update touches one row instead of many.

whys.a: A is not true, so no relationship can be "R explains A".
whys.b: A is false, so this cannot be a "both true" case.
whys.c: R is true, so the option claiming R is false is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: normalisation helps writes and integrity but often adds joins, so reads can get slower.

questions.explanation: Normalisation optimises integrity and write simplicity. Reads that need several entities pay for joins, which is why read-heavy systems denormalise selectively.

questions.prompt: Complete the definitions of the normal forms.
questions.text: Second normal form removes {1} dependencies on part of a composite key; third normal form removes {2} dependencies between non-key columns.
questions.explanation: Memory hook: 2NF = whole key, 3NF = nothing but the key. Partial = depends on part of the key; transitive = A -> B -> C where B is not a key.

questions.prompt: Match each PostgreSQL jsonb expression with what it produces or tests.

right.text: True if the left jsonb contains the right jsonb
True if the string is a top-level key
Removes the key from the document

questions.explanation: `->` keeps the jsonb type (you can keep drilling), `->>` returns text (for comparing or casting), `@>` is containment and is what a GIN index accelerates, `?` tests for a top-level key. Removal is the `-` operator.

questions.prompt: A table `events(id, payload jsonb)` is queried with `WHERE payload @> '{"type": "refund"}'` and it is slow. Which index fits best?

options.why: Right: the default `jsonb_ops` GIN class supports `@>, ?, ?| and ?&`.
A btree on jsonb only helps equality and ordering of the whole document, not containment.
It indexes a different column and a hash index cannot do containment anyway.
`BRIN` stores block ranges for naturally ordered data; it cannot answer containment.

questions.explanation: GIN for containment and key-exists. For one hot path, an expression btree such as `((payload->>'type'))` is smaller and faster. `jsonb_path_ops` is a smaller GIN class that supports only `@>` and path operators.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: The jsonb type collapses duplicate object keys, keeping the last value.
questions.reason: The json type stores an exact copy of the input text, including whitespace.

whys.a: The whitespace behaviour of json does not explain how jsonb handles duplicates.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true but about different types, so R does not explain A.
whys.c: R is true: json keeps the text as typed.
whys.d: A is true: jsonb discards duplicate keys, last one wins.

questions.explanation: jsonb parses into a binary form: no whitespace, no key order preservation, no duplicate keys, but it is indexable and faster to query. Use json only when you must keep the exact text.

questions.prompt: Write the statement that builds an index named `idx_orders_customer` on `orders(customer_id)` without blocking writes to the table.
questions.model: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
questions.explanation: Plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a `SHARE` lock that blocks writes. The concurrent form scans the table twice and lets writes continue. `IF NOT EXISTS` and `USING btree` are optional extras.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It cannot run inside a transaction block.
options.why: Right: it must be its own statement, so wrap-everything-in-a-transaction migration tools need a special case.

options.text: If it fails it can leave an `INVALID` index that must be dropped.
options.why: Right: check `pg_index.indisvalid` and drop and retry.

options.text: Normal reads and writes on the table can continue while it builds.
options.why: Right: it only takes a `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` lock.

options.text: It is faster than a plain `CREATE INDEX` on the same data.
options.why: It does two scans and waits for old transactions, so it is slower.

options.text: It takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the whole build.
options.why: That would block reads too; the entire point is to avoid it.

questions.explanation: Trade-off: slower and more fragile, but no write outage. Same applies to `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY`.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A read replica can return stale data right after a write to the primary.
questions.reason: PostgreSQL streaming replicas always apply changes synchronously before the primary acknowledges a commit.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, not merely unrelated.
whys.c: Correct: replication is asynchronous by default, so lag is possible; R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so the "A false" option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Default streaming replication is asynchronous. Fix read-your-writes by reading from the primary for a short window after a write, by sticky sessions, or by waiting for an `LSN`.

questions.prompt: A table has 10,000,000 rows. You backfill a new column with `UPDATE ... WHERE id in a range`, 5,000 rows per batch, committing after each batch. How many batches (transactions) are needed?
questions.explanation: 10,000,000 / 5,000 = 2,000. Small batches keep locks short, limit replication lag and let you throttle between batches.

questions.prompt: You must rename `users.email` to `users.contact_email` on a live system with rolling deploys. Which order is safe?

options.text: Add column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, stop old writes, drop old column.
options.why: Right: every step is compatible with both the old and the new app version.

options.text: Run `ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN` in the migration, then deploy the new code afterwards.
options.why: Old app instances still running will fail the moment the column disappears.

options.text: Deploy the new code that reads `contact_email` first, then rename the column afterwards.
options.why: The new code would query a column that does not exist yet.

options.text: Drop `email`, add `contact_email` and restore the old values from a backup file.
options.why: That loses data and causes downtime.

questions.explanation: Expand and contract: expand (add), migrate (dual write plus backfill), switch reads, contract (drop). Each deploy must work against the schema before and after the migration.

questions.prompt: Expand phase: write one statement that adds a nullable text column `contact_email` to the `users` table.

checks.label: does not make it NOT NULL

questions.model: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN contact_email text;
questions.explanation: Adding a nullable column without a default is a catalog-only change in PostgreSQL. `NOT NULL` is added at the end via a `NOT VALID` check constraint, then `VALIDATE`, then `SET NOT NULL`.

questions.prompt: Backfill step: write an `UPDATE` that copies `email` into `contact_email` for rows with `id` from 1 to 5000 that are not yet filled.
questions.model: UPDATE users SET contact_email = email WHERE contact_email IS NULL AND id BETWEEN 1 AND 5000;
questions.explanation: Idempotent, restartable batches are the point. A keyset loop (`WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000`) is an equally valid shape.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In PostgreSQL 11 and later, `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN flag boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false` does not rewrite the table.
questions.reason: A constant default is stored in the catalog and applied when old rows are read, rather than written into every row.

whys.a: Correct: the fast default is stored once and filled in on read, which explains the instant ALTER.
whys.b: R is the mechanism that makes A true.
whys.d: A is true for PostgreSQL 11+ with a non-volatile default.

questions.explanation: Volatile defaults such as `random()` or `clock_timestamp()` still force a rewrite. Before version 11 any default rewrote the whole table under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`.

questions.prompt: Table `users(id, email, deleted_at)` uses soft deletes. Write the statement that keeps `email` unique among live users only, so a deleted user's email can be reused.

checks.label: creates a UNIQUE index on users(email)
restricts it to deleted_at IS NULL

questions.model: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_live ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
questions.explanation: A partial unique index only indexes (and checks) rows matching its predicate; deleted rows are ignored. A plain `UNIQUE` constraint cannot carry a `WHERE` clause in PostgreSQL, so the index form is the answer. Verified on PostgreSQL 16.

questions.prompt: Write the PostgreSQL statements that create a table `events(id bigint, created_at timestamptz)` partitioned by range of `created_at`, and one partition `events_2025` holding all of 2025.

checks.label: creates the partition with PARTITION OF

questions.explanation: Range bounds are inclusive at FROM and exclusive at TO, so consecutive partitions tile without overlap. Verified on PostgreSQL 16. Dropping or detaching an old partition is a cheap way to expire data; a primary key on a partitioned table must include the partition key.
